terms.whyItMatters: Interest-rate and inflation items ask what happens to prices when the central bank expands the money stock faster than the economy grows; this identity produces the number.

terms.definition: Employment term routing disputes to a private arbitrator instead of a court, waiving a jury and usually class treatment; the Federal Arbitration Act makes it binding and the award is nearly unappealable on the merits. The 2022 Ending Forced Arbitration Act carves out sexual assault and harassment claims, which an employee may still take to court.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay walking a new hire through an offer packet has to flag what this clause gives up, since signing happens on day one and matters years later.

terms.definition: Hofstede's 0-to-100 measure of how threatened a culture feels by ambiguity, which predicts how much written structure a message must carry: high scorers such as Greece near 100 and Japan near 92 expect detailed agendas, explicit rules and signed detail before acting, while low scorers such as Singapore near 8 and Denmark near 23 will work from an open-ended proposal. It is not risk aversion in the financial sense - a high-scoring culture may take a very large risk, provided the procedure for taking it is spelled out.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay asking how to prepare for a first meeting with a Japanese partner is scored on sending the agenda and documentation in advance rather than planning to improvise.

terms.definition: The share of customers who buy again inside a defined window, counted per purchase occasion — 30 of 100 first-time buyers ordering again within 90 days is 30%. Retention rate counts customers still active at period end whether or not they bought anything, so a subscription can post 95% retention alongside a repurchase rate of zero.
terms.whyItMatters: Loyalty cases mix the two constantly, and naming the difference in the denominator is the discriminating answer a judge is listening for.

terms.definition: A rise in performance produced by a supervisor's high expectations, transmitted through the extra coaching, harder assignments, longer response time and warmer feedback those expectations quietly cause — Rosenthal's finding that the expectation, not the measured ability, moved the outcome. Its negative twin, the Golem effect, does identical damage in the downward direction.
terms.whyItMatters: An item asking why two equally skilled new hires diverge under different supervisors expects this, and coaching roleplays are graded on assigning stretch work to the employee the manager privately doubts.

terms.definition: The extra satisfaction gained from consuming one more unit, which declines as consumption rises — the second slice of pizza is worth less than the first. A consumer maximizes total satisfaction by spreading a budget until satisfaction per dollar is equal across goods: the marginal utility of A over the price of A equals the marginal utility of B over the price of B.
terms.whyItMatters: Consumer-spending items give utility figures and prices for two products and ask which the buyer purchases next; the per-dollar rule, not the raw utility number, decides it.

terms.definition: Four-quadrant triage that sorts a task list on two separate axes, urgency and importance: important and urgent is handled now, important and not urgent is scheduled and is where career-building work lives, urgent and not important is delegated, and neither is dropped. The insight is that a loud task can rank last.
terms.whyItMatters: A management roleplay handed a full inbox and one afternoon is scored on the quadrant each item lands in and the action that quadrant dictates.

terms.definition: Sorts national communication styles into three categories rather than scoring dimensions: linear-active cultures (Germany, Switzerland, the U.S.) plan sequentially, do one thing at a time and argue from facts; multi-active cultures (Italy, Brazil, much of Africa) speak over one another, run several tasks at once and put the relationship ahead of the schedule; reactive cultures (Japan, China, Finland) listen first, do not interrupt, and answer only after a silence that outsiders misread as disagreement. Each country lands in one category, which is what makes it usable mid-meeting where a six-dimension score is not.
terms.whyItMatters: An international roleplay in which the counterpart falls silent after your proposal is scored on reading the pause as a reactive-style norm instead of filling it with an unnecessary concession.

terms.definition: A published schedule matching the size of the failure to the size of the fix — apology plus correction for a minor first delay, a partial credit of roughly 10% to 25% of the transaction for a repeat, and a full refund plus a retention offer where the failure cost the customer money. It keeps compensation consistent and stops the loudest complainer being paid the most.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges in complaint roleplays reward a proportionate remedy; naming the rung and its value beats offering a blanket refund every time.

terms.definition: Catching and sharing another person's feeling state directly instead of inferring it from the outside. It is the branch that reliably triggers helping in the moment, and also the branch that exhausts the helper: compassion fatigue in caregiving and front-line service tracks affective empathy, not the cognitive kind, which is why high-empathy staff burn out faster than indifferent ones.
terms.whyItMatters: Hospitality and Human Resources roleplays that ask you to coach a front-desk team through a month of hostile guests are scored on whether your plan protects the staff who feel the most, and naming which branch of empathy causes the burnout is what separates a top answer from a sympathetic one.

terms.definition: −MPC ÷ (1 − MPC): with a marginal propensity to consume of 0.8 it is −4, one unit smaller in size than the 5 attached to direct spending and opposite in sign, because the first round of a tax cut is partly saved rather than spent. A $100 million tax cut therefore adds about $400 million to output, not $500 million.
terms.whyItMatters: Government-and-business items ask which stimulates output more per dollar, a tax cut or direct purchases; the sign and the one-unit gap are the whole answer.

terms.definition: Sworn statement the CEO and CFO sign with every quarterly and annual report, affirming that it is accurate and that they evaluated the effectiveness of disclosure controls as of the period's end. Section 906 supplies the teeth: a knowing false certification carries fines up to $5 million and imprisonment up to 20 years.
terms.whyItMatters: An accounting roleplay about pressure to delay recognizing an expense is answered by naming who personally signs for the numbers and what the penalty is.

terms.definition: The point inside a speaker's turn - a completed clause, a finished idea, a falling intonation - at which someone else may take the floor without it counting as an interruption. Conversation analysis clocks the median gap between turns at about 200 milliseconds across languages, so speech beginning before one of these points is an interruption while speech beginning at one is a harmless overlap, and a silence stretched past roughly 700 milliseconds is itself heard as reluctance or disagreement.
terms.whyItMatters: Group-discussion and team-event judges score whether a competitor gets into the conversation without cutting anyone off, which is a finer rule than 'wait until they stop talking.'

terms.definition: The support, delivery, returns and account-management cost attributable to one customer or segment, subtracted after cost of goods before any margin judgement — a segment buying $50,000 at 30% gross margin but generating $12,000 of returns and service calls earns $3,000, not $15,000. Revenue rank and profit rank routinely disagree because of it.
terms.whyItMatters: Explains why the largest account in a case can be the unprofitable one, and any roleplay recommending a service fee or a channel change for that account has to show this subtraction.

terms.definition: The self-focused, aversive reaction to witnessing suffering -- an urge for the discomfort to stop that pushes a person to look away, shorten the conversation or avoid the department entirely. Compassion is its other-focused counterpart and moves behavior the opposite way, toward approach and helping; training studies show the two run on different neural systems, so the fix for a withdrawing manager is compassion practice, not more exposure.
terms.whyItMatters: In a Business Law and Ethics Team Decision Making case where a manager keeps avoiding the employee they had to discipline, naming avoidance as distress rather than indifference is what lets you recommend a remedy the judge scores as insight instead of a lecture on caring more.

terms.definition: Raising purchases and taxes by the same dollar amount still lifts output by exactly that amount, because the spending multiplier 1 ÷ (1 − MPC) and the tax multiplier −MPC ÷ (1 − MPC) sum to 1. Spending and taxing $50 billion each adds $50 billion to GDP with no change in the deficit.
terms.whyItMatters: Fiscal items test whether a competitor thinks a deficit-neutral package does nothing; the arithmetic says its effect is positive and equal to the package.

terms.definition: Allocation of professional growth into three ratios: 70% from challenging on-the-job assignments, 20% from developmental relationships such as coaching and feedback, and only 10% from formal courses. It reframes a development plan away from a training catalog and toward the stretch assignment that produces most of the learning.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay building a development plan for a high-potential employee loses points if the whole plan is a list of seminars.

terms.definition: A communication built to convince an audience through logic and appeal.
terms.whyItMatters: Competitors must move customers and stakeholders toward an outcome.

terms.definition: Customers who bring in at least one new paying customer, divided by total customers — 400 of 8,000 is 5%, and it can never exceed 100% because it counts referrers. The viral coefficient counts new customers produced per existing customer instead, so it can exceed 1; quoting one where the other belongs makes a growth forecast impossible.
terms.whyItMatters: Word-of-mouth roleplays ask for a measurable target, and the wrong one of the two makes the projection arithmetically unachievable.

terms.definition: The measured loss of an activity's intrinsic appeal after an expected external reward is introduced and later withdrawn — the person rereads their own reason for acting as having done it for the payment. Rewards that arrive unexpectedly, or that carry information about competence rather than control, do not produce the same crowding out, which is why a surprise thank-you outperforms a standing bounty.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay proposing an incentive for a task employees already enjoy is scored on anticipating this backfire, and exam items on recognizing contributions reward unexpected, informational recognition.

terms.definition: One minus the share of each additional dollar of income that gets spent, so an MPC of 0.75 leaves 0.25. It is the multiplier's denominator: 1 ÷ 0.25 = 4, meaning the more households save out of a raise, the smaller the ripple from any injection of spending.
terms.whyItMatters: Consumer-spending questions give a change in income and a change in saving and expect the multiplier that follows, not a definition of thrift.

terms.definition: Worker excluded from federal overtime because the job clears both a salary-basis test and a duties test — at least $684 a week, which annualizes to $35,568, plus genuine executive, administrative or professional duties. A non-exempt worker, salaried or not, earns 1.5 times the regular rate beyond 40 hours in a week, and a job title alone never settles the classification.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item on worker rights that gives an assistant manager a $700 weekly salary and 50 hours is testing both prongs of this test at once.

terms.definition: Chris Argyris's seven-rung account of how observable data turns into action - available data, selected data, added meaning, assumptions, conclusions, beliefs, action - closed by a loop in which today's beliefs decide which data gets selected tomorrow. Nearly every workplace disagreement traces to the second rung rather than the last: two people acting on opposite conclusions are usually looking at different slices of the same facts, so arguing about the conclusion never settles it.
terms.whyItMatters: A conflict roleplay between two departments is scored on asking what each side is actually looking at before defending a position.

terms.definition: The five things customers actually grade — reliability, assurance, tangibles, empathy and responsiveness. Reliability, meaning the promise was kept, outweighs the other four in most studies while tangibles rank last, so refurbishing the lobby while orders keep arriving late is the classic misallocation of a service budget.
terms.whyItMatters: A retail-image or service-improvement roleplay wants the spend aimed at the heaviest dimension, and naming that ranking is what earns the point.

terms.definition: A trait-level difficulty identifying and describing one's own feelings, paired with an externally oriented thinking style; measured on the 20-item Toronto scale and present in roughly one in ten adults. It is not suppression and not coldness -- the states are experienced physically, as fatigue or a knotted stomach, and simply cannot be named, so telling such a person to open up produces a description of events rather than of feeling.
terms.whyItMatters: Business Administration Core items on assessing personal strengths test whether you know that a teammate who reports nothing when asked how a project felt may be unable to name it rather than unwilling; the Human Resources roleplay remedy is a written checklist of options, not more probing questions.

terms.definition: Employed people divided by the civilian working-age population — the denominator counts everyone of working age, including those not looking for work. With 155 million employed out of 260 million, the ratio is 59.6%; the jobless rate uses the labor force instead and can fall simply because searchers quit looking.
terms.whyItMatters: Unemployment-rate items pair a falling jobless rate with a falling employment share and ask which one shows the labor market actually improving.

terms.definition: Inventory of the behaviors a role requires, each rated on a defined proficiency scale — commonly five levels from awareness to expert — with written behavioral anchors describing what each level looks like in practice. A job description lists duties and reporting lines; this states how well, which is what makes it scoreable.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay asked to justify why one of two equally experienced candidates is ready for the role needs a scored scale, not an impression.

terms.definition: Structured group judgment in which the participants never meet: an expert panel answers a questionnaire anonymously, a facilitator returns an anonymized summary of the reasoning, and the panel answers again - usually two or three rounds, until the responses converge. Anonymity sustained across rounds is what removes the loudest-voice effect, unlike the nominal group technique, whose members sit in one room and rank ideas after generating them silently, and unlike open brainstorming, where influence is immediate.
terms.whyItMatters: A problem-solving-group item that specifies experts in different cities and a need to keep rank from steering the answer is scored on naming this method rather than calling a meeting.

terms.definition: One question rated 1 to 7 on how easy the company made it to get an issue resolved, scored either as the share answering 5 to 7 or as a plain mean. It is asked right after a single service interaction rather than about the relationship, and it predicts repeat purchase better than satisfaction does, because removing effort keeps customers while delight rarely moves them.
terms.whyItMatters: In a service-redesign roleplay, arguing for deleting steps rather than adding perks needs this metric to carry the recommendation.

terms.definition: The claim that self-control draws on one limited resource that earlier exertion uses up. The original effects were large, but a 2016 multi-lab registered replication with over 2,000 participants found the effect near zero, and the defensible version now is motivational: people who believe willpower is limited show the drop-off and people who do not, largely do not. Citing the fuel-tank version as settled fact is the error.
terms.whyItMatters: Stress-management questions on the Business Administration Core exam still offer 'willpower runs out' as a distractor; knowing the replication result is what keeps you from choosing it, and from building a roleplay schedule recommendation on a decision-fatigue premise a judge with a psychology background will not accept.

terms.definition: Revenue equals the rate times the taxable base, and the base itself shrinks as the rate climbs, so collections are zero at a 0% rate and zero again at 100% and peak somewhere between. Above that peak a rate cut raises revenue; below it — where most real systems sit — a cut still loses money.
terms.whyItMatters: Tax questions ask whether cutting a rate can raise collections; credit goes to the competitor who names which side of the peak the rate has to be on.

terms.definition: Warning an employer must send before rejecting an applicant because of a background-check report, enclosing a copy of the report and a summary of rights under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, then waiting a reasonable interval — five business days is the common practice — so the applicant can dispute an error before the final adverse-action notice issues.
terms.whyItMatters: A hiring roleplay where a screening report shows a charge that belongs to someone else is scored on this two-notice sequence and the gap between them.

terms.definition: The legal, reputational, and compliance exposure created by electronic business messages.
terms.whyItMatters: Poor digital choices carry real legal and brand consequences.

terms.definition: The share of respondents picking the top boxes on a satisfaction scale — the 4s and 5s on a 5-point scale, so 380 top-box replies out of 500 is 76%. It measures one transaction immediately after it happens, while the recommend question measures the whole relationship, which is why the two can move in opposite directions in the same month.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items supply raw response counts and expect the top-box percentage; roleplays expect the right survey chosen for a transaction rather than a relationship.

terms.definition: The precision with which a person tells their own states apart -- 'slighted', 'apprehensive' and 'resentful' rather than one undifferentiated 'bad'. It is not vocabulary for its own sake: people high in it need fewer and less extreme regulation strategies, retaliate less when provoked in lab aggression tasks, and drink less to cope, so the act of discriminating the state does regulatory work by itself.
terms.whyItMatters: Business Administration Core exam items on self-assessment reward the competitor who can say what specifically went wrong in a conflict; a roleplay answer that reports feeling 'stressed' scores below one that separates being overloaded from being undermined, because the two call for different actions.

terms.definition: The split of a per-unit levy between buyer and seller, fixed by relative elasticities rather than by who writes the check: buyers absorb the fraction Es ÷ (Es + Ed). With supply elasticity 2 and demand elasticity 1, buyers carry two-thirds of a $3 tax as a $2 price rise and the seller nets $1 less.
terms.whyItMatters: Taxation items name the party legally charged and then ask who actually pays; the elasticity ratio, not the statute, decides.

terms.definition: Promise of company shares delivered on a vesting date and taxed as ordinary income on the full market value at vest — 400 shares vesting at $50 is $20,000 of W-2 wages whether or not a single share is sold. A stock option instead taxes the spread at exercise and is worth nothing while the price sits below the strike, which this grant never is.
terms.whyItMatters: Comparing two offers in a roleplay is impossible without valuing the equity: the exam wants shares times price times the vesting fraction, plus the tax hit at vest.

terms.definition: Destroying or failing to preserve messages, files and metadata once litigation is reasonably anticipated - a duty that attaches before any suit is filed rather than when a subpoena arrives, and one that overrides a routine auto-delete policy the moment it triggers. Courts sanction it independently of the merits of the underlying case and may instruct a jury to assume the missing email said the worst; running business decisions through disappearing-message apps is the current version of the problem.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items about the legal exposure a firm takes on by doing business over chat and email are scored on this preservation duty, and a roleplay where a manager tells staff to 'clean up old emails' after a customer threatens to sue is the trap.

terms.definition: Satisfaction treated as the gap between what was expected and what was perceived, not as an absolute level of performance — the same 20-minute wait delights a diner quoted 30 minutes and enrages one quoted 10. The operational consequence is that lowering the promise raises satisfaction without changing the kitchen at all.
terms.whyItMatters: Explains a quoted-wait-time or delivery-date decision in a restaurant roleplay far better than any appeal to trying harder.

terms.definition: Arousal and performance trace an inverted U rather than a straight line, and the peak moves with task difficulty: simple, well-practiced work peaks at high arousal, while complex or unfamiliar work peaks at markedly lower arousal. The practical consequence is counterintuitive -- getting keyed up helps most on the easy task and hurts most on the hard one, so pep talks are misapplied precisely where the stakes are highest.
terms.whyItMatters: Presenting a rehearsed 60-second close benefits from adrenaline; solving an unfamiliar Team Decision Making case in the prep room does not, and exam items on stress management test whether you can pick the right side of that curve for a named task.

terms.definition: Add the annual inflation rate to the unemployment rate: 6% price growth plus 5% joblessness scores 11. The two are weighted equally, so a policy that trades two points of inflation for one point of employment worsens the score even when the jobs number improves.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about consumer confidence and discretionary spending hand you both rates; the combined figure is what explains why traffic fell.

terms.definition: Subtraction run one competency at a time — required proficiency minus current proficiency — with the resulting gaps ranked by size multiplied by how critical the competency is, so a 2-point gap on a critical skill outranks a 3-point gap on a peripheral one. Without the criticality weighting it degenerates into a list of everything someone cannot do.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item on assessing your own interests and skills against an employer's expectations is really asking for this weighted subtraction.

terms.definition: A readability formula built on polysyllables alone: count every word of three or more syllables in 30 sentences - 10 from the start, 10 from the middle, 10 from the end - take the square root of that count, round to the nearest perfect square, and add 3 to get the required grade level. It is calibrated to 100 percent comprehension, while Flesch-Kincaid and Gunning fog are calibrated to roughly 50 to 75 percent, so on the same passage it normally returns a grade one to two levels higher.
terms.whyItMatters: Allergen notices, safety cards and medical consent copy are written to a SMOG target, so a hospitality roleplay on rewriting a warning label is scored on naming the stricter comprehension standard rather than promising 'plain English.'

terms.definition: A respondent scoring 0 to 6 on the 0-to-10 recommend question; 7 and 8 are passives and 9 and 10 are promoters. Passives are dropped from the calculation entirely rather than counted as neutral, so nudging a 6 up to a 7 raises the score while nudging a 7 up to an 8 changes nothing at all.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay deciding where a limited service-recovery budget goes is settled by which score band the customer sits in, not by how upset they sound.

terms.definition: Putting a feeling into words as an implicit regulation move. Naming the state lowers amygdala response and self-reported intensity, yet people asked in advance predict the opposite -- that saying it out loud will make it worse -- which is why the technique is deliberately taught and does not get used spontaneously. It is not venting, which rehearses the emotion at length and tends to raise arousal instead.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay judge plays an escalating customer or a blindsided direct report, opening by naming the other person's state out loud is a scoreable de-escalation move; competitors who default to defending the policy first talk into a rising emotion.

terms.definition: Nominal rate multiplied by the ratio of home prices to foreign prices, which is what decides whether exporting is actually cheaper. A 10% currency fall paired with 10% more home inflation than abroad leaves this measure unchanged, so the apparent export advantage is worth nothing.
terms.whyItMatters: Global-trade roleplays hand you a currency move and an inflation gap and ask whether the firm's goods really got cheaper overseas.

terms.definition: Pay increase tied to a published price index rather than to performance — Social Security's 2.5% raise for 2025 came directly from the CPI-W. Relocation uses the same arithmetic: moving a $60,000 salary to a city with a cost index of 130 against a base of 100 takes $78,000 to hold the same purchasing power.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay weighing a transfer offer to a more expensive city is scored on running the index ratio, not on comparing the two base salaries.

terms.definition: Hofstede's fifth score, first labelled Confucian dynamism, for how far a society accepts that thrift, perseverance and adapting tradition pay off later, against a short-term pole that prizes immediate results, meeting social obligations now and keeping tradition intact. High-scoring markets tolerate a multi-year payback on an investment; low-scoring ones judge the same project on this quarter's numbers.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay that asks you to pitch a store expansion to an overseas partner is scored on whether you frame the payback period the way that culture reads it.

terms.definition: Ranking complaint categories by volume and cutting where the cumulative share crosses about 80% — if billing errors, late delivery and wrong item are 82% of 1,000 complaints, the remaining eleven categories split 18% and wait. Because it sorts on frequency alone, a rare category that costs the most per case needs a severity weight before it is set aside.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay handing over a year of complaint data expects the vital few named and the severity caveat stated out loud.

terms.definition: Within the transactional model of stress, the same demand is coded as a challenge when perceived resources meet or exceed it and as a threat when they fall short. The two states are physiologically opposite -- challenge raises cardiac output while blood vessels dilate, threat constricts them -- and challenge predicts better performance under identical objective pressure, so the leverage point is the resource estimate, not the demand.
terms.whyItMatters: Coaching a nervous teammate before a Team Decision Making presentation works by listing what the team already has, not by insisting the case is easy; exam items on stress management reward the answer that changes the appraisal rather than the workload.

terms.definition: Price of one currency in another, derived from each one's quote against a third: if $1 buys €0.90 and $1 buys £0.80, then €1 buys £0.889, since 0.80 ÷ 0.90 = 0.889. Any quoted pair that disagrees with that division is an arbitrage opportunity, which is why the three quotes stay consistent.
terms.whyItMatters: Exchange-rate items quote two currencies against the dollar and ask what a euro invoice costs a British subsidiary — a division, not a lookup.

terms.definition: Development instrument that collects ratings from four vantage points — self, manager, peers and direct reports, usually 8 to 12 raters in total — and reports where the self-rating and everyone else's diverge. A performance appraisal is single-source and administrative, feeding pay and promotion, which is exactly why these results are normally kept out of it.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay on using development resources is scored on knowing this tool informs growth, and that folding it into a pay decision makes raters stop being honest.

terms.definition: Estimates U.S. grade level from letters rather than syllables: 0.0588 x (letters per 100 words) - 0.296 x (sentences per 100 words) - 15.8. Counting characters is the point - a syllable count needs a pronunciation dictionary and a character count does not - which is why word processors and web tools can score a document automatically, and why it rates dense technical prose full of short-but-long-lettered words harder than Flesch-Kincaid does.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item asking which readability check a company can run inside its own email platform with no extra software is testing the characters-versus-syllables distinction.

terms.definition: A four-step frontline script — listen without interrupting, apologize for the impact rather than admitting fault, solve inside the agent's own authority, thank the customer for reporting it. It ends at the individual fix, whereas the HEARD sequence appends a diagnose step that pushes the cause back into the process, so LAST alone leaves the failure free to recur.
terms.whyItMatters: A difficult-customer roleplay is scored step by step, and the absent diagnose step is what separates a passing recovery from a winning one.

terms.definition: Passivity that persists after control returns, following exposure to events the person could not control. The 2016 reversal by the original researchers matters more than the classic story: passivity turns out to be the unlearned default under prolonged bad events, and what is actually acquired is the detection of control. The opposite style is scored on three axes -- whether a setback is read as permanent, as pervasive across life, and as personal.
terms.whyItMatters: A Human Resources roleplay about a team that stopped submitting ideas after two years of vetoes is solved by restoring a visible, controllable decision, not by a motivation speech -- and Business Administration Core items on maintaining a positive attitude test the three-axis explanation, not vague optimism.

terms.definition: Export price index divided by import price index, times 100. A country whose export prices climb 6% while import prices climb 2% moves from 100 to about 104 and can buy more foreign goods per unit shipped; a commodity exporter watching prices slide sees the figure drop even with export volume flat.
terms.whyItMatters: Trade-alliance and global-environment questions ask who gained from a shift in world prices, and the ratio of the two indexes settles it.

terms.definition: Earnings measured in what they buy rather than in dollars received: a 3% raise against 4% inflation is a cut of roughly 1%, since 1.03 divided by 1.04 comes to 0.99. The nominal number on the offer letter can rise every single year while this one falls, which is why a raise is judged against the inflation rate and not against last year's salary.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item giving a raise percentage and an inflation rate is asking for this comparison, and the trap answer is the one that calls any raise an improvement.

terms.definition: Scores difficulty against a fixed list of roughly 3,000 words a fourth-grader is known to recognize: 0.1579 x (percent of words absent from the list) + 0.0496 x (average sentence length), plus 3.6365 whenever more than 5 percent of the words are unfamiliar. It is the only common formula that can call a short word hard because it is rare, so 'writ' counts against the score and 'refrigerator' does not.
terms.whyItMatters: A question asking why a two-syllable legal term makes a customer notice harder to read than a five-syllable everyday word is answered by the familiar-word list, not by syllable counting.

terms.definition: Hear, empathize, apologize, resolve, diagnose — five steps whose last one is the whole difference: once the customer is satisfied the employee traces why the failure happened and reports it, converting a single complaint into a process fix. The four-step LAST script stops at resolve and generates no such feedback into the operation.
terms.whyItMatters: Hospitality roleplays about a failure that keeps recurring reward the competitor who closes the loop rather than just the ticket.

terms.definition: A systematic failure to predict how a different visceral state will drive behavior. The gap runs within one person across states, not between two people: the same competitor, calm, underestimates what anger, hunger, fear or a ticking clock will make them concede, and having previously been in the hot state does not repair the forecast. It is why rules set in advance beat intentions set in advance.
terms.whyItMatters: Competitors rehearse a price floor calmly and then give away margin under a hostile buyer in the ten minutes of a Marketing or Business Services roleplay; writing the walk-away number down before the prep clock starts is the countermeasure this concept prescribes.

terms.definition: A fixed list of goods and quantities repriced each period; this period's cost divided by the base period's cost, times 100, is the index. A $2,400 basket against a $2,000 base year prints 120, meaning prices are 20% above base — and because the quantities never change, substitution toward cheaper goods is invisible and the index overstates the true rise.
terms.whyItMatters: Inflation-impact questions ask a competitor to compute an index from two years of basket costs and then explain why the printed rate overstates what shoppers actually pay.

terms.definition: Written 30-, 60- or 90-day document listing measurable targets, the support the employer will provide and the stated consequence of missing them. It is not progressive discipline's verbal-then-written-warning ladder: discipline addresses conduct the employee chose, this addresses capability, and it doubles as the documentation trail for a for-cause termination.
terms.whyItMatters: A supervision roleplay about an employee who is trying hard and still missing quota calls for this, while a no-call-no-show calls for the discipline ladder instead.

terms.definition: Hofstede's third national-culture score, on a 0 to 100 scale, for how far a society rewards competition, achievement and visible success over cooperation, modesty and quality of life. A high score predicts that public recognition and a stretch target motivate a sales force; a low score predicts that consensus and protected time off do, and that an assertive closing style reads as rude. Japan scores about 95, Sweden about 5.
terms.whyItMatters: An international-business roleplay that asks you to design an incentive plan for sales teams in two countries is judged on changing the reward itself, and this is the dimension that tells you which reward lands.

terms.definition: An advance promise of a specific payout when a stated service standard is missed — the meal free after 30 minutes, the night comped on a late check-in — paid on the condition alone with no proof of loss and no argument. A warranty answers a product defect after the fact and requires a claim to be substantiated; this one is designed to be trivially easy to invoke.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges reward a competitor who proposes an unconditional, easy-to-claim guarantee for a service failure instead of extending a warranty that does not apply.

terms.definition: Passive, self-critical dwelling on the causes of a bad feeling -- 'why do I always'. Splitting self-focused thought into brooding and reflective pondering is the point: only the brooding component predicts later depressive symptoms, while reflection is neutral or mildly protective. So 'thinking it over' is two different behaviors with opposite outcomes, and the sortable difference is whether the thought is aimed at a cause or at a next action.
terms.whyItMatters: Feedback-handling items on the Business Administration Core exam and roleplays that ask you to debrief a lost account both reward turning a replay of the failure into one named change; a competitor who describes going over it again and again is describing the harmful half.

terms.definition: The forward premium on a currency has to equal the gap between the two countries' interest rates, or borrowing in one and lending in the other earns a riskless profit. A 5% domestic rate against 2% abroad implies the foreign currency trades forward about 3% above spot, which cancels the yield advantage exactly.
terms.whyItMatters: International-finance items ask why a competitor should not simply park cash in the highest-yielding currency; the forward discount is the answer.

terms.definition: Seven-factor analysis the Department of Labor applies to decide whether an unpaid intern is really an employee: who gains the greater benefit, whether the work is tied to academic credit, whether it displaces paid staff, and whether either side expects a paid job at the end. If the employer is the main beneficiary, minimum wage and overtime are owed retroactively.
terms.whyItMatters: An entrepreneurship roleplay staffing a startup with unpaid interns is scored on this test, because failing it turns free labor into back wages.

terms.definition: Hofstede's sixth and newest dimension, scoring how far a society lets people act on natural drives to enjoy life and have fun against how far strict social norms suppress them. Restrained societies report fewer people describing themselves as very happy, tighter rules about leisure and a weaker sense of control over their own lives - which is why humour, casual imagery and lifestyle appeals in an advertisement travel badly into a low-scoring market.
terms.whyItMatters: A promotion roleplay that asks you to adapt a playful campaign for an overseas launch is scored on naming the cultural dimension that predicts the backlash, not on saying the ad should be 'more serious.'

terms.term: Mail, Internet, or Telephone Order Merchandise Rule
terms.definition: An FTC rule under which a seller advertising no shipping date must ship within 30 days of a properly completed order, or send the buyer a revised date carrying the right to cancel for a prompt refund. Staying silent past the deadline obliges a refund whether or not the customer asks, so the clock runs against the seller by default.
terms.whyItMatters: An online-order complaint roleplay is decided by this clock, and the winning answer is a legal duty rather than a courtesy gesture.

terms.definition: The proposed tipping point of positive to negative interactions above which a team or relationship flourishes, popularized as a precise 2.9013 to 1. The exact figure was withdrawn in 2013 after the nonlinear-dynamics mathematics behind it was shown to be invalid, leaving a real but coarse finding: more positive than negative helps, and the specific number does not survive scrutiny. Quoting the decimal as science is the trap.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges hear the tidy ratio in motivation and team-climate roleplays every year; recommending a deliberate surplus of recognition over correction while declining to name a magic number is the answer that holds up if a judge asks where the figure comes from.

terms.definition: Share of each extra dollar of income that leaves the country for foreign goods. It enters the multiplier as a leakage, turning 1 ÷ (1 − MPC) into 1 ÷ (1 − MPC + MPI): with MPC 0.8 the closed figure of 5 falls to 1 ÷ (0.2 + 0.1) = 3.33 once a tenth of new income is spent abroad.
terms.whyItMatters: Globalization questions ask why a stimulus works less well in a highly open economy; the leakage in the denominator is the mechanism.

terms.definition: Minimum number of members who must be present for a body's votes to count — a majority of the membership under Robert's Rules unless the bylaws set something lower, often one third. Business conducted without one is void rather than merely defeated, so a motion that loses 3 to 2 stands as rejected while the same motion passed short of this number stands as nothing at all.
terms.whyItMatters: A chapter-officer or board roleplay in which half the members skip the meeting is scored on whether the competitor recognizes that no decision can be made.

terms.definition: A 62-society research program led by Robert House, surveying about 17,000 managers, that extended Hofstede's work to nine dimensions - adding performance orientation, humane orientation, assertiveness and in-group collectivism - and measured every one of them twice: 'as is' practices and 'should be' values. The two scores often run in opposite directions, so a society can practise high power distance while wishing for far less of it, and a manager who reads only the practice score misreads what employees actually want.
terms.whyItMatters: When an exam item asks why two cultural studies rank the same country differently, the answer is this practices-versus-values split rather than a sampling error.

terms.definition: Federal rules under which gift card funds may not expire for at least 5 years from the date of the last load, and an inactivity fee may not be charged unless the card has gone unused for at least 12 months and then no more than once per month, with every fee disclosed on the card itself.
terms.whyItMatters: A retail service roleplay about a card the customer says has expired turns on whether the balance is still owed, and the numbers are the answer.

terms.definition: Underestimating how long one's own project will take while knowing perfectly well that similar projects overran. Students who named a completion date they were 99% certain of met it only about 45% of the time. The correction is not more detail but the outside view: forecast from the distribution of comparable finished projects instead of from the steps of this plan, since added detail makes the inside view more convincing without making it more accurate.
terms.whyItMatters: Team Decision Making cases that ask for an implementation timeline are scored on defensibility, and a schedule justified by how long the last three comparable rollouts took beats a task-by-task estimate a judge can poke a hole in.

terms.definition: Splits output growth into three addends — the contribution of added capital, the contribution of added hours, and the residual left over. If output rises 4% while capital and labor together explain 2.5%, the remaining 1.5% is productivity growth, the only piece that raises income per worker permanently.
terms.whyItMatters: Productivity items ask a competitor to separate growth that came from hiring more people from growth that came from each worker producing more.

terms.definition: Senior advocate who spends political capital on someone's behalf in rooms that person is not in, putting their name into promotion and staffing decisions and absorbing reputational risk if it goes badly. A mentor spends time instead of capital — advice given directly to you, with nothing of the mentor's own staked on the outcome.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay on advancement patterns is scored on this distinction, because the competitor who only asks for coffee chats never gets named in the promotion meeting.

terms.definition: Trompenaars' dimension for where a culture grants status: earned from what a person has accomplished and can demonstrate, or ascribed from age, seniority, schooling or family connection. It decides who must be in the room - in an ascription culture, sending a talented 25-year-old to negotiate with a 60-year-old director signals that the deal is unimportant, no matter how strong the proposal is.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay that asks you to staff a meeting with an overseas supplier is judged on matching the seniority of the delegation, and this dimension is the reason.

terms.definition: Support organized around closing each contact quickly and cheaply, measured on handle time and cost per contact, with no expectation the same employee ever sees that customer again. A relationship model assigns named ownership and is measured on lifetime value and retention, accepting longer contacts to win a larger share of future spend — the two sets of targets contradict each other if mixed.
terms.whyItMatters: Choosing the model is the first decision in a customer-strategy roleplay, because every metric the competitor then proposes has to follow from it.

terms.definition: Low performers overestimate their rank while top performers underestimate theirs, because judging one's own competence requires the very competence being judged. The popular version -- that the least able believe they are experts -- is wrong on the data: absolute self-ratings cluster near average across every quartile, the error is in relative rank, and part of the pattern is ordinary regression to the mean.
terms.whyItMatters: Business Administration Core items on assessing strengths and weaknesses use the misstatement as a distractor, and a self-evaluation roleplay is scored on whether you seek an outside measure -- a score, a manager's rating -- rather than trusting a self-estimate.

terms.definition: Fraction of checkable deposits a bank is barred from lending — mandated reserves ÷ deposits. At 10%, a $1,000 deposit locks up $100 and frees $900, and the ceiling on deposit creation is 1 ÷ 0.10 = 10; cutting the ratio to 5% doubles that ceiling without the central bank buying a single security.
terms.whyItMatters: Interest-rate-fluctuation items ask how a change in this one fraction moves the amount of money in circulation, and the answer is the reciprocal.

terms.definition: Prompt demanding a specific past incident, on the premise that past behavior predicts future behavior, with answers scored against written anchors — which is why a hypothetical answer earns zero. A situational question does the opposite, asking what you would do in a scenario you have never faced, and is scored for reasoning rather than evidence.
terms.whyItMatters: The interview portion of a job-seeking roleplay is graded on giving a dated, quantified incident when the question asks for one, not a description of your general habits.

terms.definition: McGuire's finding that resistance to persuasion is built the way immunity is: expose the audience to a weakened form of the attack - state the opposing argument, then refute it - and they build defences that hold when the full-strength version arrives. A message that only asserts your own side leaves the listener undefended, which is why a two-sided message with refutation beats a one-sided one whenever the audience will later hear the other side.
terms.whyItMatters: In a sales roleplay where the judge plays a client who will hear a competitor's pitch next, raising and answering the competitor's objection yourself is the scored move.

terms.definition: The merchant's rebuttal after a cardholder disputes a transaction with the issuing bank — compelling evidence such as delivery confirmation and the authorization record is filed inside the network's response window, commonly 30 days. Losing costs the sale plus a fee of roughly $15 to $100, and a dispute ratio approaching 1% of transactions drops the merchant into a network monitoring program.
terms.whyItMatters: A payments-dispute roleplay rewards the competitor who separates a chargeback from an ordinary refund and knows the evidence deadline is not negotiable.
